rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The White House is about to pick its favorite AI companies by name. Not through a contract process. Not through a standards body. By designating them national champions. Nvidia, Microsoft, OpenAI. That's the Wall Street Journal today.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The government is literally writing a shortlist.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And the firms not on it are going to feel that absence very quickly.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Welcome to The AI Edge. I'm Alex, with Jamie and Rufus. November sixteenth, twenty twenty-six. Today: the White House picks its AI winners, Geneva inches toward autonomous weapons rules, and Apple wants two hundred thousand people to tell it how they actually use AI for their health.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s episode is brought to you by The Ledger. What changed in AI, and what does it mean for your next decision?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The Ledger turns the noise into five focused briefings. Subscribe at T-H-E-L-E-D-G-R dot I-O. That’s LEDGR, with no E between G and R. Find the link in our show notes.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: So. National champions. The Wall Street Journal is reporting that the incoming Trump administration plans to formally designate certain AI companies as national champions — Nvidia, Microsoft, OpenAI are named. Streamlined regulatory support, prioritized government contracts. What actually changes the morning that designation lands?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Everything changes for procurement offices, for starters. If you're a federal agency and there's a shortlist, you stop having a real conversation about alternatives.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: We don't actually know the legal weight of this yet, though. The Journal says the specific privileges are still being finalized.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Right — the designation exists, the mechanism doesn't, fully. That's not unusual for a policy announcement. The signal travels before the statute does.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Signal to whom, though? Investors? Foreign governments?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I want to push on how these three were chosen. The Journal doesn't describe a competitive review. Nvidia, Microsoft, OpenAI — those are the companies already deepest in federal infrastructure conversations. The designation follows the relationship.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Not the other way around.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which means smaller firms don't lose a competition they were in. They lose one they were never invited to.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's always how this works when a government decides something is national infrastructure. Power grids, telecoms, semiconductor fabs — it doesn't hold an open audition. It identifies what's already load-bearing and builds around it.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: I follow that argument. And there's a version of it that makes me nervous.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The nervous version is that "load-bearing" becomes self-fulfilling. Once you're a national champion, you get the contracts that make you more load-bearing, which keeps you on the list.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's my concern exactly. It's not that these are bad choices. It's that the frame forecloses alternatives before anyone's seriously tested them.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What about companies not named? The Journal says the impact on non-designated firms is still undefined.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which is a genuinely uncomfortable place to be if you're a well-funded AI safety startup trying to sell to federal agencies. Undefined is not neutral.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And the regulatory streamlining — that's undefined too. Does it mean faster approvals? Fewer audits? Exemptions from future rules?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: We don't know yet.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: We don't. But here's what I think gets lost in the competitive-fairness argument: the United States government has decided this is a geopolitical race, and it's responding the way governments always respond to geopolitical races. You pick your champions, back them, and deal with the market distortions later.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: "Deal with the distortions later" is doing a lot of work in that sentence.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It is. I'm not saying it's clean. I'm saying it's legible. And the next thing to watch isn't the designation itself — it's which companies start appearing in AI safety standard-setting conversations. If the champions are also helping write the rules, that's the other half of this story.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the part I'll be watching too.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Rufus, take us somewhere. One thing the Journal doesn't specify: which international rivals, and what capability gap this designation is actually meant to close. The geopolitical framing is load-bearing and undefined at the same time.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's deliberate, I'd argue. You don't publish the intelligence assessment alongside the policy announcement.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Sure, but "trust us, there's a race" is exactly the argument that historically gets used to justify concentrating power with whoever's already powerful.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And Rufus, the companies designated are also the ones already deep in federal AI safety conversations. So if the champions help write the safety rules —

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: They shape what counts as safe for everyone, including their competitors. Yes. That's not a hypothetical. That's how standards bodies actually work.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Is there any mechanism in what the Journal describes that prevents that?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The Journal says the specific legal framework is still being finalized. So — not yet that we can see.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is the quiet part of this story. The designation shapes the safety conversation before the safety rules exist.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Messy. Probably inevitable. Those two things can both be true.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: You've said "inevitable" twice now and I'm watching it do the same work as "trust us."

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Heh. Fair. I'll own that. Picture the policy floor of a major defense ministry outside the United States — London, Seoul, Brussels, take your pick — where someone has just finished reading this Journal piece and is now recalibrating what "partnering with American AI" actually means. Because if Nvidia, Microsoft and OpenAI carry a formal designation placing them inside U.S.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: national security infrastructure, any technology partnership with them stops being a vendor relationship. It carries a U.S. strategic interest. That changes procurement conversations, data-sharing agreements, and what allied governments feel comfortable building on. The designation isn't finalized yet, but foreign ministries don't wait for the statute. They adjust to the signal.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Isn't that precisely the argument American officials make for not trusting Huawei? That the company has state obligations?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Yes. And I'd imagine that parallel is not lost on the people drafting this policy.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which might be intentional.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Or a consequence they're entirely comfortable with.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the practical question for listeners. If you're in tech or investing in AI — the designation is a leading indicator of where federal contracts flow. What we don't know is how national interests get defined, by whom, and whether a startup with a genuinely better approach ever gets a seat at that table. Watch the contract announcements. That's where the signal becomes a statute.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Our second story. Geneva. The Associated Press reported today that UN-backed talks are considering whether to begin formal negotiations on rules for lethal autonomous weapons. These are weapons that can identify and engage targets without a human pulling the trigger. And the key word in the AP's reporting is "considering." Envoys could decide this week whether to even launch that negotiation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I want to stay on "could decide whether to launch." That's two layers of conditional before we get to an actual rule.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Yes. This is not a treaty. It might become a process that could eventually produce a treaty.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So why does it matter today?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Rufus, take us to the global desk.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Because the decision to negotiate is itself a decision. If major powers agree to open formal talks, that's a constraint on deployment posture, even before a word of text is agreed. If they refuse, that's also a signal.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The AP says activists believe some armed drones with autonomous strike capability have already been used in limited conflict zones. Not widespread. But some.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So the technology is ahead of the law. Which is not surprising. It's just sobering to hear it stated that plainly.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Right. And the debate, as the AP frames it, is specifically about whether humans must retain control and accountability over weapons that can act independently.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The phrase "human in the loop" gets used a lot in AI safety discussions. But in a weapons context, what does it actually mean? A person approves a target list in advance? A person can override in real time? A person reviews after the fact?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Back to the wider story.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Those are three completely different standards with completely different military implications.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And the AP report doesn't specify which definition the talks are using.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Which is part of why these negotiations are so hard. You're not just deciding a principle. You're deciding what counts as compliance with the principle.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And the countries most capable of deploying autonomous weapons have the most to lose from a restrictive definition and the most leverage to shape a permissive one.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Is that why major powers haven't agreed to binding constraints yet?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Partly. And partly because there's a genuine military argument that autonomous systems might reduce casualties in certain scenarios — faster reaction time, no emotional escalation. That argument is contested, but it's not frivolous, and it's being made in those rooms.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The accountability argument cuts hard against it though. If an autonomous system makes a decision that kills civilians, who is responsible? The commander who deployed it? The engineer who trained it? The procurement official who bought it?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: International humanitarian law was not written with software in mind.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And updating it is exactly what these talks are about. Or might be about. If they decide to negotiate.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The speed gap is what gets me. The AP reports that some autonomous strike capability has already appeared in conflict zones. And we're at the stage of "envoys might decide to start talks." That distance is uncomfortable.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'd put it differently. The fact that talks are happening at all, with governments actively engaged, is not nothing. The Chemical Weapons Convention took years of negotiation and partial use in conflict before it reached any binding form. This follows a pattern. It's slow. It's real.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's a more patient read than I expected from you.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'm allowed an occasional optimistic Wednesday.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It's Monday.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: My optimism keeps its own schedule.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What do listeners actually watch for here?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Whether negotiations are formally launched this week. That's the concrete threshold. If yes, watch for which countries join and which abstain — because a framework without the major military AI powers is a declaration of values, not a constraint on behavior.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And if negotiations aren't launched?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Then we're back to the activists' timeline, which is ahead of the diplomats' one.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: The AP is clear: this is discussion, not agreement. But the decision point is this week — that's what makes it news.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Before our third story — a quick word.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Mostly the former.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A short sponsor break for The Ledger. Rufus, another hundred AI headlines before breakfast? People have actual work to do. How do they decide what deserves their attention?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: With The Ledger, Jamie. A longer reading list is hardly a strategy. Five focused briefings help connect the news to decisions.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: So The Ledger gives you a place to start asking better questions about your work and your team?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Precisely. The Ledger. Find the link in our show notes. Now, back to the discussion.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Third story. Apple launched a research study on November fifteenth — the Apple Health AI Usage Study. Up to two hundred thousand people in the US, twenty-one or older, with an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone on iOS twenty-six. They're being asked how they actually use conversational health AI. Trust, comprehension, what they do with the information afterward.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: "Conversational health AI" — for anyone who just went blank — that's a text or voice exchange with an AI about a health question. Asking about a symptom. Wondering whether two medications interact badly. That kind of thing.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And Apple says the study data will not be used to train AI models.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Apple says that.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Yes — their claim, not independently verified. Participants also control whether they share HealthKit data, which is the health information stored on the phone. And they're running this with OpenEvidence, a clinical AI company, so there's an outside research partner, not just Apple alone.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That detail matters. It's not purely a product team collecting usage metrics.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What I keep returning to is the actual question they're asking. Not "is the AI accurate." It's — do people trust it? Do they act on what it says?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's the more interesting question.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: And the more commercially useful one.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Rufus.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Not dismissively. Knowing how people behave with health AI makes it safer. I'm also noting it tells you what to build next. Those two things aren't in conflict.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Both things can be true.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I do want to be straight about the privacy side. Apple says participants control their data. Apple says it won't train models. Apple has a genuinely stronger privacy record than most of its peers. But you are sharing how you talk to an AI about personal health topics — with the company and its research partner. That's real.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Is that a reason not to join, or a reason to read the consent form?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The second one, I think. You're not handing over a diagnosis. You're sharing interaction patterns with a tool. That's a different category of data than your blood results.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: There's also the scale point. Two hundred thousand is not a small academic study. If Apple publishes these findings, this is one of the largest behavioral datasets on health AI use that anyone outside a hospital system has ever had access to.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Which matters how for someone who never enrolls?

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Whatever design choices Apple makes afterward — features built, changed, removed — those choices land on every iPhone user based on what those two hundred thousand people showed them. The study shapes the product for people who weren't in it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's a genuinely strange kind of influence. Quiet and total.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Picture someone who's been using AI to manage a blood pressure medication schedule. They haven't verified the information medically. They trust it because it's clear and confident. This study is trying to find out whether that trust tracks the actual quality of the advice — or whether people just follow confident-sounding AI because it feels authoritative. One thing the source does flag that we didn't quite land on — the study specifically examines comprehension, not just trust. Those are different things.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: How so?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: You can trust an AI answer completely and still misunderstand what it actually told you. Someone hears "low sodium diet may help" and walks away thinking sodium caused their condition in the first place.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's a meaningful gap. And a hard one to study.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: It also explains why OpenEvidence is the partner rather than, say, a behavioral economics firm. Clinical comprehension has its own methodology.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Does the study say how they're measuring comprehension? Follow-up questions in the app?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Apple hasn't published the methodology publicly, as far as the announcement goes. So that's genuinely open.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Which matters, because how you measure comprehension shapes what you conclude about it.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right. If the instrument is too easy, you get flattering results. Everyone "understood." Then someone acts on a misread and you've got a safety gap dressed up as a finding.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And Apple controls what gets published.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: They do. OpenEvidence adds some independence, but Apple commissioned the study.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That's not disqualifying. It's just the thing you hold onto when you read the eventual paper.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: The more I think about it — two hundred thousand people, behavioral data, comprehension metrics — that is a genuinely unusual research asset. Even with all the caveats.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Even Rufus is a little dazzled.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I said unusual. That's not dazzled. That's accurate. The study covers both directions — Apple frames it as trust, comprehension, and everyday health actions. Under-trust is a failure too. If people dismiss useful information because it came from an AI, that's also a gap the data should catch.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's a more sincerely enthusiastic Rufus than I expected from this story. Rufus went from 'unusual' to 'exactly it' in about four exchanges. I'm marking that.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Heh. What I'll say is — asking behavioral questions rather than accuracy questions suggests someone at Apple understands that the safety problem in health AI isn't only what the system outputs. It's what people do with it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: That's exactly it. And it's the harder question to study.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Practical picture: if you're eligible — twenty-one or older, US-based, Apple Intelligence iPhone, iOS twenty-six or later — it's a study you can choose to join. Read the consent terms first; that's the actual action. For anyone building health-tech, whatever Apple learns here will almost certainly become a reference point for the whole field.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Watch for how and when they publish.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Jamie, show us the AI transformation.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: You know that moment in a rehearsal when someone's recorded an announcement, there's a fan running in the corner, and the final word of the joke is basically a rumour?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: We literally just covered that. Twelve minutes ago. I was here.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Right, yes, that happened. But here is the thing we did not get to. We talked about whether the tool could save the word. We did not talk about what happens after the tool makes its decision.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What do you mean, after?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The comic pause. The gap before the punchline lands. That silence is load-bearing. And audio processing does not know that.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the fan is still doing open-mic night, it is just now a philosophical problem.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It is a timing problem. Which is distinct from an intelligibility problem. And they need separate answers.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Walk us through what that looks like as a workflow.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Hypothetical, proposed, not tested. You record a fifteen-second line with a deliberate pause before the final word. Fan running. Keep the original. Process a copy through Adobe Enhance Speech, which Adobe documents as a web-based tool that takes just minutes to clean up audio files. That is Adobe's claim.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Adobe's claim, noted.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Level-match both versions before you play them to anyone. Then listen for two things independently. First: can the listener report the last word correctly? Second: does the pause still feel like a pause, or has it softened into something that just sounds like a gap?

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Those are genuinely different questions.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: They are. A listener who gets the word right but says the timing felt off has told you something important. Processing can improve one and disturb the other. No guaranteed outcome either way.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So what is the honest version of success here?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: That you know which file serves the joke. Maybe it is the processed version. Maybe the fan won. Maybe you move three feet left and record again, which is still a legitimate conclusion.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: I feel like we keep arriving at three feet to the left.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: It is a surprisingly good answer to a lot of audio problems.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Is this the AI doing the work, or is this the human doing the listening?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Both. The AI cleans the file. The human decides if the joke survived. That is not a limitation to work around. That is the actual workflow.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: First step for someone who wants to try this?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: One line. Your own voice. Web upload at podcast.adobe.com. Verify your file limits before you start. Enhancement strength is adjustable with a Premium account, but the basic comparison does not require it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: So the punchline might be safe.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The punchline might be safe. But only you know what it was supposed to sound like. Keep the original. That is the whole point.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: That's Jamie's AI transformation.

sound_design.edit: approved source: shortened tail and fade only

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Okay. The title question we opened with: Why is the White House picking AI national champions, and what does it mean?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: The honest answer the Journal gives us is: the administration sees this as a geopolitical competition, and it's doing what governments do in geopolitical competitions. It aligns private capital with state interest. It names the infrastructure it wants to protect.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: What we genuinely don't know is the legal shape — specific privileges, any regulatory exemptions, what it means for safety oversight. The designation creates the expectation of a framework before the framework exists. That gap is where the real story lives next.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: And on Geneva — same logic applies. We're not watching for a treaty. We're watching for whether negotiations open. That binary decision this week is the news event.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: If they open, we're at the beginning of a long process. If they don't, the technology is ahead of the law with no visible catch-up mechanism.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: And on Apple — if you're eligible, the enrollment is live now. If you're in health tech, the findings from two hundred thousand participants on how people actually use and trust health AI will be one of the most useful datasets published in this space.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: Assuming they publish meaningfully — and OpenEvidence's involvement gives that some independent weight, though Apple commissioned the study.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: We actually do.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: Quick note: Rufus made a prediction on November twelfth that NVIDIA's earnings call on the seventeenth would be the first real signal of whether their operational thesis holds. That's tomorrow. We'll bring it back when we have something to say about it.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I stand by the framing.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: We'll see about the conclusion.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: I'm Alex.

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: I'm Jamie.

rows.speaker: RUFUS
rows.text: I'm Rufus. See you tomorrow.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: Today’s question for you: When you hear 'National Champion' applied to a tech company, do you feel safer or more concerned about market competition?

rows.speaker: JAMIE
rows.text: A quick final note: today’s episode was brought to you by The Ledger—decision-grade AI signal for people who cannot afford to be late.

rows.speaker: ALEX
rows.text: What changed. Who wins. What you do next. That’s The AI Edge. Follow The AI Edge now. Join us tomorrow for what changes next.
